claims.text: The starting composite contains discrete W particles or an interconnected W ligament network in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation and interfacial voids.
A uniform, ultra-thin Cr layer should be deposited on W surfaces before composite consolidation.
A surface coating can be deposited by magnetron sputtering.
Atomic layer deposition is an example of physical vapor deposition suitable for the proposed Cr coating.
The Cr interlayer will act as a stable diffusion barrier at W–Cu interfaces.
The Cr interlayer will act as a reactive interfacial agent that strengthens bonding between W and Cu.
Excessive interdiffusion between W and Cu leads to phase separation and void nucleation.
The Cr coating inhibits excessive diffusion between the W and Cu phases.
Controlling interfacial reactions with Cr prevents weak boundary regions and interfacial voids.
A coherent, well-bonded W–Cu interface supports efficient thermal conduction under high temperature and irradiation.
Coating-assisted interface engineering has improved interfacial bonding in an analogous coated-particle composite.
Cr-coated W–Cu will exhibit less phase separation during processing and service than untreated W–Cu.
Cr-coated W–Cu will exhibit fewer interfacial voids during processing and service than untreated W–Cu.
Cr-coated W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu under high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
Phase separation and interfacial voids lower the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu under high heat flux and irradiation.
The intervention is expected to remain effective through typical powder-metallurgy or sintering consolidation and subsequent high-heat-transfer and irradiation service.
